Pathology 04.question: ১) Which herpes virus causes Kaposi's sarcoma?
Pathology 04.exp:
Kaposi’s sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also called Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus (KSHV).

  • HHV-6 → Roseola infantum (classically)

  • HHV-8 → Kaposi’s sarcoma

  • EBV (HHV-4) → Infectious mononucleosis, Burkitt lymphoma, etc.

  • CMV (HHV-5) → Opportunistic infections, congenital CMV

Exam pearl:
Kaposi’s sarcoma → HHV-8.

Pathology 04.question: ২) Which one is the most important test for recent infection with HBV?
Pathology 04.exp:
IgM anti-HBc (IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen) is the most important marker of recent/acute HBV infection.

  • IgM anti-HBc → recent/acute infection; may also appear during a flare of chronic HBV.

  • IgG anti-HBc → indicates previous or ongoing infection and persists for life.

  • IgM/IgG anti-HBe → not the primary marker used to identify recent infection.

High-yield HBV recall:
Recent/acute HBV infection → IgM anti-HBc

Exam pearl:
“Recent HBV infection” → think IgM anti-HBc.

Pathology 04.question: ৩) Which one is pathognomonic for measles?
Pathology 04.exp:
Koplik’s spots are considered pathognomonic/classically characteristic of measles. They appear as tiny bluish-white spots on an erythematous background, typically on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, shortly before the skin rash.

  • Generalized maculopapular rash: Characteristic of measles but not pathognomonic.

  • Giant cell pneumonia: Can occur as a severe complication, especially in immunocompromised patients.

  • SSPE: A rare, late neurological complication of measles.

Exam pearl:
Measles → Koplik's spots.

Pathology 04.question: ৪) Which is the most common insect borne viral disease in the world?
Pathology 04.exp:
Dengue is the most common mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide. It is mainly transmitted by Aedes aegypti and, to a lesser extent, Aedes albopictus.

  • Dengue: Mosquito-borne viral disease; very widespread globally.

  • Rabies: Mainly transmitted through bites of infected mammals, especially dogs—not an insect-borne disease.

  • Chikungunya: Also mosquito-borne, but less common globally than dengue.

  • Measles: Transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets/aerosols, not insects.

Exam pearl:
Most common insect/mosquito-borne viral disease → Dengue.

Pathology 04.question: ৫) The definitive diagnosis of HIV can be done by which analysis method?
Pathology 04.exp:
Traditionally, Western blot was used as a confirmatory test for HIV after a reactive screening test such as ELISA.

  • ELISA: Mainly a screening test for HIV antibodies/antigen.

  • RIA: Not the standard confirmatory method.

  • Western blot: Historically used for confirmation of HIV infection.

  • Southern blot: Used for detecting specific DNA sequences, not routine HIV diagnosis.

High-yield HIV recall:
ELISA → Screening
Western blot → Confirmatory (classical exam answer)

Exam pearl:
For this traditional MCQ, Western blot is the expected answer.
Note: Modern HIV diagnostic algorithms generally use antigen/antibody immunoassays followed by differentiation assays and, when needed, HIV-1 NAT rather than Western blot.

Pathology 04.question: ৬) Which species of staphylococcus usually causes UTI?
Pathology 04.exp:
Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a well-known cause of urinary tract infection (UTI), particularly in young sexually active women. It is an important cause of community-acquired UTI after E. coli.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • S. aureus: Can cause UTI, especially in hospitalized patients or with bacteremia, but is not the usual cause.

  • S. epidermidis: Mainly associated with catheter/prosthetic device-related infections.

  • S. histolyticum: Not a typical cause of UTI.

High-yield Microbiology recall:
Young woman + UTI → Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

Exam pearl:
Common Staphylococcus causing UTI = S. saprophyticus.

Pathology 04.question: ৭) Streptococcus pneumoniae are chiefly found in.....?
Pathology 04.exp:
Streptococcus pneumoniae commonly colonizes the upper respiratory tract, particularly the nasopharynx and oropharynx. Among the given options, oropharynx is the expected answer.

It is an important cause of:

  • Pneumonia

  • Meningitis

  • Otitis media

  • Sinusitis

Exam pearl:
S. pneumoniae → normal colonizer of upper respiratory tract, especially nasopharynx/oropharynx.

Pathology 04.question: ৮) HSV-2 leads to latent infection in which ganglia?
Pathology 04.exp:
HSV-2 primarily causes genital herpes and establishes lifelong latency in the sacral sensory nerve ganglia, especially the sacral dorsal root ganglia.

  • HSV-1 → Trigeminal ganglion → commonly associated with oral herpes

  • HSV-2 → Sacral ganglia → commonly associated with genital herpes

Exam pearl:
HSV-2 → Sacral ganglion; HSV-1 → Trigeminal ganglion.

Pathology 04.question: ৯) Which hepatitis virus is a defective virus?
Pathology 04.exp:
HDV is a defective/satellite virus because it cannot complete its life cycle independently. It requires HBV, specifically HBsAg, to provide the envelope needed for viral assembly and transmission.

  • HAV: Complete virus

  • HBV: Complete virus

  • HCV: Complete virus

  • HDV: Defective virus; requires HBV

High-yield Hepatitis recall:
HDV + HBV → severe hepatitis
HDV cannot infect/replicate effectively without HBV.

Exam pearl:
Defective hepatitis virus = HDV.

Pathology 04.question: ১০) Which is not true about polio virus?
Pathology 04.exp:
Poliovirus belongs to the Picornaviridae family and is a non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus.

  • Non-enveloped → True

  • ssDNA → False; poliovirus is ssRNA (+)

  • Fecal-oral transmission → True

  • Humans are the only natural reservoir → True

High-yield Virology recall:
Poliovirus = non-enveloped + positive-sense ssRNA + fecal-oral transmission + human reservoir.

Exam pearl:
Polio is an RNA virus, not a DNA virus → ssDNA is the incorrect statement.

Pathology 04.question: ১১) Super antigen produced by staphylococcus aureus is involved in the pathogenesis of which one of the following disease?
Pathology 04.exp:
Staphylococcus aureus produces superantigens, particularly TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome toxin-1), which plays a major role in the pathogenesis of toxic shock syndrome.

TSST-1 causes massive, nonspecific T-cell activation by cross-linking MHC class II molecules with T-cell receptor Vβ regions, leading to a large release of cytokines → fever, hypotension, rash, and multiorgan dysfunction.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • Impetigo: Mainly due to exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB) or S. pyogenes.

  • Septicemia: Not classically mediated by a superantigen.

  • Scalded skin syndrome: Caused by exfoliative toxins (ETA/ETB), which target desmoglein-1.

High-yield Microbiology recall:
S. aureus → TSST-1 (superantigen) → Toxic shock syndrome.

Exam pearl:
Superantigen of S. aureus = TSST-1 → Toxic shock syndrome.

Pathology 04.question: ১২) Which disease is caused by clostridium perfringens?
Pathology 04.exp:
Clostridium perfringens commonly causes food poisoning, especially after eating improperly cooked or stored meat and gravy.

  • C. tetani → Tetanus

  • C. botulinum → Botulism

  • C. difficile → Pseudomembranous colitis

  • C. perfringens → Food poisoning + gas gangrene

High-yield Microbiology recall:
C. perfringens → Food poisoning + Gas gangrene (myonecrosis).

Exam pearl:
Clostridium perfringens → Food poisoning.

Pathology 04.question: ১৩) At least....... fold rise in antibody titer in acute & convalescent sera is diagnostic for dengue?
Pathology 04.exp:
For dengue, a fourfold or greater rise in antibody titre between acute and convalescent serum samples is considered diagnostic of recent infection.

  • 2-fold → insufficient

  • 3-fold → insufficient

  • 4-fold → diagnostic

  • 5-fold → also exceeds the threshold, but not the standard cutoff

Exam pearl:
Acute vs convalescent serum → ≥4-fold rise in antibody titre = diagnostic of dengue.

Pathology 04.question: ১৪) Which is a protease inhibitor drug used in treatment of HIV infection?
Pathology 04.exp:
Indinavir is a protease inhibitor (PI) used in antiretroviral therapy for HIV.

  • Indinavir → Protease inhibitor

  • Abacavir → NRTI

  • Tenofovir → NRTI

  • Lamivudine → NRTI

High-yield HIV drug recall:
Protease inhibitors: Indinavir, Ritonavir, Saquinavir, Lopinavir, Atazanavir, Darunavir.

Exam pearl:
Indinavir = HIV protease inhibitor.

Pathology 04.question: ১৫) Which is the main site of colonization of staphylococcus aureus?
Pathology 04.exp:
The anterior nares (nose) are the main site of colonization of Staphylococcus aureus. Around 20–30% of healthy people may carry S. aureus in the nose at a given time.

  • Nose → primary/commonest colonization site

  • Skin and perineum can also be colonized.

  • Mouth is not the principal site.

Exam pearl:
Staphylococcus aureus → anterior nares (nose).

Pathology 04.question: ১৬) Which one is known as spreading factor for streptococcus?
Pathology 04.exp:
Hyaluronidase is known as the “spreading factor” of Streptococcus. It breaks down hyaluronic acid in connective tissue, facilitating the spread of bacteria through tissues.

  • Hyaluronidase → Spreading factor

  • Streptokinase → Fibrinolysis; helps bacteria spread through clots

  • DNase → Breaks down DNA in pus

  • Streptolysin → Hemolytic toxin

Exam pearl:
Streptococcus spreading factor = Hyaluronidase.

Pathology 04.question: ১৭) HSV-1 causes all of the following except.....?
Pathology 04.exp:
HSV-1 commonly causes:

  • Gingivostomatitis → common primary oral infection

  • Herpes labialis → recurrent “cold sores”

  • Encephalitis → HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis in adults

Genital herpes is classically caused by HSV-2, although HSV-1 can also cause genital herpes, especially through oral-genital transmission.

Exam pearl:
For classical MCQs: HSV-1 → oral lesions & encephalitis; HSV-2 → genital herpes.

Pathology 04.question: ১৮) Which of the following indicates active viral replication of HBV?
Pathology 04.exp:
HBeAg (hepatitis B e antigen) indicates active HBV replication and is generally associated with high infectivity.

  • HBsAg → Current HBV infection

  • HBeAg → Active viral replication + high infectivity

  • Anti-HBc → Previous or current infection; IgM indicates recent infection

  • HBcAg → Not routinely detectable in serum

Exam pearl:
Active HBV replication → HBeAg.

Pathology 04.question: ১৯) What is the shape of capsid of rabies virus?
Pathology 04.exp:
Rabies virus belongs to the Rhabdoviridae family and has a characteristic bullet-shaped virion.

  • Rabies virus → Bullet-shaped

  • Enveloped, negative-sense ssRNA virus

  • Has a helical nucleocapsid

Exam pearl:
Rhabdovirus = Bullet-shaped virus.

Pathology 04.question: ২০) Which one is coagulase positive staphylococcus?
Pathology 04.exp:
Staphylococcus aureus is the classical coagulase-positive Staphylococcus.

  • S. aureus → Coagulase positive

  • S. epidermidis → Coagulase negative

  • S. saprophyticus → Coagulase negative

Exam pearl:
Coagulase-positive Staphylococcus = S. aureus.

Pathology 04.question: ২১) Which group of herpes virus commonly causes congenital & perinatal infections?
Pathology 04.exp:
Among the herpesviruses, CMV (HHV-5) is the most important cause of congenital and perinatal infections.

  • CMV → congenital infection → hearing loss, microcephaly, intracranial calcification, developmental problems

  • HSV-2 → neonatal herpes, commonly acquired during delivery from an infected mother

  • HSV-1 → mainly oral infection and encephalitis

  • EBV → infectious mononucleosis and certain malignancies

Exam pearl:
Most important herpesvirus causing congenital infection = CMV.

Pathology 04.question: ২২) Which hepatitis virus infection is important cause of post transfusion hepatitis?
Pathology 04.exp:
HCV is an important cause of post-transfusion hepatitis because it is primarily blood-borne and can be transmitted through contaminated blood or blood products.

  • HAV → fecal-oral transmission

  • HCV → blood-borne; important cause of post-transfusion hepatitis

  • HDV → requires HBV coinfection/superinfection

  • HEV → mainly fecal-oral transmission

Exam pearl:
Post-transfusion hepatitis → HCV.

Pathology 04.question: ২৩) Negri body is important in laboratory diagnosis of which disease?
Pathology 04.exp:
Negri bodies are eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in neurons, particularly in the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum, in rabies infection.

They represent accumulations associated with rabies viral replication.

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • AIDS: Diagnosed by HIV antigen/antibody tests and nucleic acid testing.

  • Dengue: Diagnosed by NS1 antigen, RT-PCR, or serology.

  • Leprosy: Diagnosed by clinical findings, slit-skin smear, and biopsy.

Exam pearl:
Negri bodies → Rabies.

Pathology 04.question: ২৪) Which tumor is most common in AIDS patient?
Pathology 04.exp:
Kaposi's sarcoma is a classic and important AIDS-associated malignancy, caused by HHV-8. It commonly presents with violaceous/purple skin or mucosal lesions and may involve internal organs.

  • Kaposi's sarcoma → HHV-8 → AIDS-associated tumor

  • Burkitt lymphoma → EBV-associated; also increased in HIV

  • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma → EBV-associated

  • Oral hairy leukoplakia → EBV-associated lesion, but it is not a tumor

Exam pearl:
Classic/common AIDS-associated tumor = Kaposi's sarcoma.

Pathology 04.question: ২৫) Which is the 1st serological marker to appear in serum even before biochemical & clinical evidence of hepatitis?
Pathology 04.exp:
HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen) is the first serological marker to appear in the blood after HBV infection. It can become detectable before clinical symptoms and biochemical evidence such as elevated ALT/AST.

  • HBsAg → First marker to appear

  • HBeAg → Indicates active viral replication and high infectivity

  • Anti-HBs → Appears later and indicates immunity/recovery

  • HBcAg → Not routinely detectable in serum

High-yield HBV recall:
HBV infection → HBsAg appears first → HBeAg → anti-HBc → anti-HBs appears during recovery.

Exam pearl:
First serological marker of HBV infection = HBsAg.

Pathology 04.question: ২৬) HIV virus preferentially infects & kills which portion of T lymphocyte?
Pathology 04.exp:
HIV preferentially infects and progressively destroys CD4⁺ T-helper lymphocytes.

HIV binds to the CD4 receptor, with CCR5 or CXCR4 serving as important co-receptors for viral entry. Progressive loss of CD4 cells leads to immunodeficiency and AIDS.

  • CD4 → primary target of HIV

  • CD8 → cytotoxic T cells; not the primary target

Exam pearl:
HIV → CD4⁺ T-helper cell destruction → immunodeficiency.

Pathology 04.question: ২৭) Which group of streptococcus is leading cause of neonatal sepsis?
Pathology 04.exp:
Streptococcus agalactiae, also known as Group B Streptococcus (GBS), is a major cause of neonatal sepsis, especially early-onset neonatal sepsis.

Transmission commonly occurs vertically from a colonized mother to the newborn during labor or delivery.

  • S. agalactiae (Group B) → Neonatal sepsis/meningitis

  • S. pyogenes (Group A) → Pharyngitis, skin infections, rheumatic fever

  • Viridans streptococci → Dental caries, subacute endocarditis

  • S. faecalis (Enterococcus) → UTI, nosocomial infections, endocarditis

Exam pearl:
Neonatal sepsis → Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae).

Pathology 04.question: ২৮) Which clostridium species is responsible for gas gangrene?
Pathology 04.exp:
Clostridium perfringens is the most common cause of gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

It produces powerful toxins, especially alpha toxin (lecithinase/phospholipase C), causing:

  • Muscle necrosis

  • Hemolysis

  • Gas production in tissues

  • Severe systemic toxicity

Why the other options are incorrect:

  • C. tetani → Tetanus

  • C. botulinum → Botulism

  • C. difficile → Antibiotic-associated diarrhea/pseudomembranous colitis

Exam pearl:
Gas gangrene → Clostridium perfringens.

Pathology 04.question: ২৯) Which is not true about corynebacterium diphtheriae?
Pathology 04.exp:
Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, pleomorphic, club-shaped bacillus, not a Gram-negative rod.

  • Gram-positive rods → True

  • Club-shaped appearance → True

  • Airborne droplet transmission → True

  • Diphtheria antitoxin is used in treatment → True

Exam pearl:
C. diphtheriae = Gram-positive, club-shaped bacillus → diphtheria.

Pathology 04.question: ৩০) Which is the route of transmission for enteric fever?
Pathology 04.exp:
Enteric fever (typhoid/paratyphoid fever) is caused by Salmonella Typhi and Salmonella Paratyphi and is transmitted mainly through the faecal–oral route, usually by contaminated food or water.

  • Faecal–oral → Correct

  • Blood → Not the primary route of transmission

  • Sexual contact → Not a usual route

  • Air droplets → Not a usual route

Exam pearl:
Enteric fever → faecal–oral transmission → contaminated food/water.

Pathology 04.question: ৩১) Which one is second week symptom of enteric fever?
Pathology 04.exp:
Rose spots are a characteristic feature of the 2nd week of enteric (typhoid) fever. They are small, faint, pink, blanching macules, typically found on the trunk, especially the abdomen and chest.

Typical progression:

  • 1st week: Fever, headache, malaise, myalgia; relative bradycardia may develop.

  • 2nd week: Rose spots, abdominal symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly, and increasing toxicity.

  • 3rd week: Complications such as intestinal hemorrhage or perforation may occur.

Exam pearl:
2nd week of enteric fever → Rose spots on the trunk.

Pathology 04.question: ৩২) Which is not a usual Complications of typhoid fever?
Pathology 04.exp:
Common complications of typhoid (enteric) fever include:

  • Gut perforation → classically due to ulceration of Peyer’s patches, usually in the terminal ileum.

  • Cholecystitis → Salmonella Typhi can colonize the gallbladder.

  • Meningitis → rare but recognized, particularly in severe infection.

Appendicitis is not a usual/classic complication of typhoid fever.

Exam pearl:
Typhoid complications → intestinal hemorrhage/perforation + cholecystitis + rare CNS complications; appendicitis is not a usual complication.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৩) In a patient with typhoid fever spleen becomes palpable on..?
Pathology 04.exp:
In enteric (typhoid) fever, splenomegaly commonly develops during the second week, and the spleen may become palpable around the 7th–10th day.

High-yield Typhoid timeline:

  • 1st week: Step-ladder fever, headache, malaise, abdominal symptoms

  • 7th–10th day: Splenomegaly becomes palpable

  • 2nd week: Rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly, increasing toxicity

  • 3rd week: Intestinal hemorrhage/perforation may occur

Exam pearl:
Typhoid → palpable spleen around 7th–10th day.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৪) Which one is not correct regarding trismus in tetanus?
Pathology 04.exp:
Trismus (lockjaw) is a characteristic early feature of tetanus, caused by sustained spasm of the masseter and other muscles of mastication.

  • Spasm of masseter muscles → True

  • Difficulty opening the mouth → True

  • Difficulty in mastication → True

  • Very painful condition → Not typically described as the defining feature; the sustained muscle spasms can be painful, but trismus itself is classically characterized by rigidity and restricted mouth opening.

Exam pearl:
Tetanus → trismus (lockjaw) = masseter spasm + inability/difficulty to open the mouth.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৫) Which is not a cardinal features of Hansen's disease?
Pathology 04.option3: Acid fast bacilli on skin smears
Pathology 04.exp:
The cardinal features of Hansen’s disease (leprosy) are:

  • Anaesthetic skin lesions

  • Thickened peripheral nerves with sensory/motor loss

  • Demonstration of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear

Although Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, the causative organism is not itself a cardinal clinical/diagnostic feature.

Exam pearl:
Cardinal signs of leprosy = anaesthetic skin lesion + thickened peripheral nerve + AFB on slit-skin smear.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৬) All of the following nerves are damaged in leprosy except..?
Pathology 04.exp:
In leprosy (Hansen’s disease), Mycobacterium leprae characteristically affects superficial peripheral nerves, especially those that are relatively superficial and cooler.

Commonly affected nerves include:

  • Great auricular nerve

  • Radial nerve

  • Common peroneal (common fibular) nerve

  • Ulnar nerve — most commonly affected

The anterior tibial nerve is not a typical nerve affected in leprosy.

Exam pearl:
Leprosy → Ulnar, great auricular, common peroneal, radial (superficial branches) nerves are commonly involved.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৭) What is the duration of treatment according to Modified WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (MDT) regimens for Multibacillary leprosy?
Pathology 04.exp:
According to the WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen, multibacillary (MB) leprosy is treated for 12 months.

The standard MB-MDT regimen includes:

  • Rifampicin

  • Clofazimine

  • Dapsone

High-yield Leprosy recall:
MB leprosy → MDT for 12 months
PB leprosy → MDT for 6 months

Exam pearl:
Multibacillary leprosy → 12 months of WHO MDT.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৮) Which anti TB drug causes 8th nerve damage?
Pathology 04.exp:
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside and can cause ototoxicity, affecting the 8th cranial nerve (vestibulocochlear nerve).

It may cause:

  • Vestibular toxicity → vertigo, imbalance

  • Cochlear toxicity → hearing loss

High-yield Anti-TB drug adverse effects:

  • INH → Peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis

  • Rifampicin → Orange-red body fluids, hepatitis

  • Streptomycin → 8th nerve toxicity, nephrotoxicity

  • Ethambutol → Optic neuritis (2nd cranial nerve)

Exam pearl:
8th cranial nerve damage → Streptomycin.

Pathology 04.question: ৩৯) Which is not a cause of false negative tuberculin test?
Pathology 04.exp:
A false-negative tuberculin (Mantoux) test can occur when cell-mediated immunity is suppressed, such as in:

  • HIV/AIDS → impaired cellular immunity

  • Malnutrition → impaired immune response

  • Malignancy → immunosuppression/anergy

Previous BCG vaccination does not cause a false-negative Mantoux test. In fact, BCG vaccination may cause a false-positive tuberculin test, particularly when vaccination was recent.

Exam pearl:
False-negative Mantoux → HIV + malnutrition + malignancy; BCG vaccination → may cause false-positive.

Pathology 04.question: ৪০) Which one is the pulmonary complication of pulmonary TB?
Pathology 04.exp:
Aspergilloma (fungus ball) is a well-known pulmonary complication/sequela of pulmonary tuberculosis. It commonly develops within a pre-existing TB cavity, where Aspergillus colonizes the cavity.

  • Aspergilloma → pulmonary complication/sequela of TB

  • Laryngitis → extrapulmonary TB involvement

  • Amyloidosis → systemic complication of chronic TB

  • Empyema necessitans → can occur as a complication of TB but is less classically the answer in this MCQ

Exam pearl:
Old pulmonary TB cavity + Aspergillus colonization → Aspergilloma.

Pathology 04.question: ৪১) Treatment duration of severe case of extrapulmonary TB is..?
Pathology 04.exp:
For severe extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB), treatment is generally extended to 12 months, depending on the site and clinical circumstances.

Examples of severe EPTB include:

  • TB meningitis

  • TB of bone and joints

  • Other complicated forms of extrapulmonary TB

High-yield TB recall:

  • Most drug-sensitive TB → 6 months

  • TB meningitis / severe EPTB → commonly 9–12 months, depending on guideline and site.

Exam pearl:
Severe extrapulmonary TB → 12 months is the expected answer for this MCQ.

Pathology 04.question: ৪২) Which is the absolute indication of steroids along with anti-TB drugs?
Pathology 04.exp:
Corticosteroids are strongly indicated with anti-TB therapy in tuberculous meningitis because they reduce meningeal inflammation, cerebral edema, and the risk of neurological complications and death.

  • Tubercular meningitis → Definite/absolute indication for adjunctive steroids

  • Tubercular peritonitis → Steroids are not routinely indicated.

  • Tuberculous pericarditis → Steroids may be considered in selected cases, but they are not an absolute indication.

  • Bilateral adrenal TB → Requires glucocorticoid replacement if adrenal insufficiency is present, but this is different from adjunctive steroids for TB inflammation.

Exam pearl:
TB meningitis + anti-TB drugs → add corticosteroids.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৩) Deficiency of which vitamin is a risk factor for Tuberculosis?
Pathology 04.exp:
Vitamin D deficiency is associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis (TB). Vitamin D plays an important role in cell-mediated immunity, particularly macrophage activation against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • Vitamin D deficiency → increased risk/susceptibility to TB

  • Vitamins B, C and K are not the classic answer in this context.

Exam pearl:
Vitamin D deficiency → increased risk of tuberculosis.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৪) Which drug is used for the elimination of luminal cyst in amoebic dysentry?
Pathology 04.exp:
In amoebic dysentery (amoebiasis), drugs are often used in two steps:

  1. Tissue amoebicide → Metronidazole/Tinidazole

    • Eliminates Entamoeba histolytica from tissues and controls invasive disease.

  2. Luminal amoebicide → Diloxanide furoate

    • Eliminates luminal cysts and helps prevent recurrence/transmission.

Why the others are less appropriate:

  • Metronidazole → Mainly a tissue amoebicide; should generally be followed by a luminal agent.

  • Tinidazole → Similar to metronidazole; mainly tissue-active.

  • Nitazoxanide → Not the standard first-line luminal amoebicide.

Exam pearl:
Luminal cyst eradication in amoebiasis → Diloxanide furoate.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৫) Which one is causative organism for bacillary dysentery?
Pathology 04.exp:
Bacillary dysentery is classically caused by Shigella species, especially Shigella dysenteriae.

  • Shigella → Bacillary dysentery

  • Entamoeba histolytica → Amoebic dysentery

  • Giardia lamblia → Giardiasis

  • Balantidium coli → Balantidial dysentery

Exam pearl:
Bacillary dysentery = Shigella.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৬) Which is not a usual complication of diphtheria?
Pathology 04.exp:
Important complications of diphtheria include:

  • Laryngeal obstruction → due to the diphtheritic membrane, potentially causing airway compromise.

  • Myocarditis → an important systemic complication of diphtheria toxin.

  • Peripheral neuropathy → may occur due to toxin-mediated nerve damage.

Laryngeal oedema is not usually listed as a characteristic complication of diphtheria; the classic airway complication is laryngeal obstruction from the pseudomembrane.

Exam pearl:
Diphtheria complications → airway obstruction + myocarditis + peripheral neuropathy.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৭) Serotype O139 of cholera established in which year?
Pathology 04.exp:
Vibrio cholerae O139 (Bengal) emerged and was first recognized in 1992 during an epidemic in southern India and Bangladesh.

It was notable because it caused epidemic cholera similar to V. cholerae O1, but possessed a distinct O-antigen.

High-yield Microbiology recall:

  • O1 → classical major cholera serogroup

  • O139 Bengal → emerged in 1992

Exam pearl:
V. cholerae O139 Bengal → 1992.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৮) Which is the best fluid for intravenous replacement in Cholera?
Pathology 04.exp:
Ringer-Lactate (RL) is the preferred IV fluid for severe dehydration due to cholera because its electrolyte composition closely approximates the losses caused by profuse cholera diarrhea.

  • Ringer-Lactate → preferred

  • Normal saline → can be used if RL is unavailable

  • 5% DNS → not the preferred initial fluid for cholera dehydration

  • Hartmann's solution → essentially another name for lactated Ringer's solution, so this option is also chemically equivalent in many formulations

Exam pearl:
Severe dehydration in cholera → IV Ringer-Lactate is the fluid of choice.

Pathology 04.question: ৪৯) Which one is the most important diagnostic method in enteric fever?
Pathology 04.exp:
Blood culture is the most important and definitive diagnostic test for enteric (typhoid) fever, especially during the first week of illness.

  • Blood culture → Gold-standard/definitive diagnosis; detects Salmonella Typhi/Paratyphi.

  • Widal test → Limited sensitivity/specificity; not preferred where culture is available.

  • Urine culture → May become positive later but is less sensitive.

  • CBC → Nonspecific findings such as leukopenia may occur.

Exam pearl:
Enteric fever → Blood culture = most important diagnostic test.

Pathology 04.question: ৫০) Whooping cough is caused by which organism?
Pathology 04.exp:
Whooping cough (pertussis) is caused by Bordetella pertussis, a small Gram-negative coccobacillus.

The characteristic “whoop” occurs due to repeated episodes of forceful coughing followed by a deep inspiratory sound.

  • B. pertussis → Whooping cough

  • Legionella pneumophila → Legionnaires’ disease

  • H. influenzae → Meningitis, epiglottitis, etc.

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa → Opportunistic infections

Exam pearl:
Whooping cough = Bordetella pertussis.
